Special Tickets in the Valley of the Kings: Seti I, Tutankhamun and Which Are Worth It

Seti I, Tutankhamun or Ramesses VI? Which extra Valley of the Kings tickets earn their price, what they cost and how to fit them into a morning

22 November 2026 · 9 minute read

By Islam Hussein, Sillage Égypte journey designer. Last updated: November 2026.

The quick answer

Three extra tickets in the Valley of the Kings are worth considering: Seti I (KV17) for the finest carved and painted relief in the valley, Ramesses V and VI (KV9) for its painted ceilings and modest price, and Tutankhamun (KV62) for the king himself rather than the walls. If you buy only one, make it KV9 on a budget and KV17 if the New Kingdom is why you came. Tombs close for conservation from time to time, so confirm status the week you travel. Prices are as reported in November 2026.

Key facts

Ticket Price for a foreign adult (as reported November 2026) Status Our verdict
General Valley of the Kings ticket EGP 750, for three of the open tombs Open 06:00 to 17:00 Enough for most mornings
Seti I (KV17) EGP 2,000, on top of the general ticket Listed as open in July 2026 Worth it for anyone serious about the New Kingdom
Ramesses V and VI (KV9) EGP 220, on top of the general ticket Listed as open in July 2026 The best value on this page: ceilings worth the climb alone
Tutankhamun (KV62) EGP 700, on top of the general ticket Listed as open in July 2026 Worth it once: you come for the king himself, not the decoration
Nefertari (QV66), Valley of the Queens Not on sale Reported closed since March 2024, no reopening date Plan without it

Every Valley of the Kings visitor meets the same arithmetic at the same ticket window. The general ticket, reported at EGP 750 for a foreign adult, admits you to three of the open royal tombs, and three are enough for most mornings. Three tombs sit outside it, each with its own ticket: Seti I, Tutankhamun, and Ramesses V and VI. Whether they are worth the extra money is the question travellers ask most often on a west-bank morning. The honest answer is yes for all three, for different reasons, and the deciding factor is rarely the price. Sillage Égypte (sillage-egypte.com), the private Egypt journey designer, plans west-bank days around these tickets, and this is our advice.

Is Seti I's tomb worth it? (KV17)

Yes, if you care about how the walls were made. The Tomb of Seti I (KV17) is the longest tomb in the Valley of the Kings, about 137 metres cut into the limestone. Giovanni Battista Belzoni found it on 16 October 1817, and the world had seen nothing like it.

Here is the reason to pay: the tomb is decorated in painted raised relief, the figures carved so that they stand proud of the wall before the colour was laid on, with one side chamber as the exception. The Litany of Ra runs down the early corridor, where Seti stands before Ra-Horakhty, and the Book of Gates fills the pillared chamber and the burial chamber. Stand at the top of the descent after the second stairwell, where the corridor falls away below you, and look down the whole decoration programme at once.

It is also the most expensive of the valley's tickets, at EGP 2,000 on top of the general ticket. The tomb reopened to the public on 1 November 2016 after several years closed, so ask on the day about access and photography. For a first-time visitor with one west-bank day, that money can sometimes go further elsewhere, but if Seti I is why you came to Luxor, do not leave wondering. The valley closes tombs for conservation, and KV17 has closed before, so confirm its status the week you travel.

Is Tutankhamun's tomb worth the extra ticket? (KV62)

Honestly, yes once, with adjusted expectations. The Tomb of Tutankhamun (KV62) is small, probably begun for a non-royal person and adapted when the young king died, around 1323 BC, and its walls are modest beside the giants around it. Only the burial chamber is decorated, and one scene has entered the canon: Ay, the successor, performing the opening-of-the-mouth ritual before the mummy.

The reason to buy the ticket is that Tutankhamun himself is still there. His mummy has lain in a climate-controlled glass case in the tomb since 2007, and the sarcophagus remains in the burial chamber. You are paying EGP 700 to stand in the place where a New Kingdom king was laid to rest, while the treasures that filled these rooms are displayed at the Grand Egyptian Museum in Giza. The story does the work: the 1922 discovery, Howard Carter, the sealed door, the dynasty that died with him. Come for the history rather than the painting, and the ticket pays for itself.

Ramesses V and VI: the best value in the valley (KV9)

The Tomb of Ramesses V and VI (KV9) is the one to buy when you can afford only one extra ticket. Begun for Ramesses V and taken over by Ramesses VI, it costs a modest EGP 220.

Walk down looking up, not sideways. The ceilings carry the Book of the Day and the Book of the Night, framed by the sky goddess Nut arching over you. The walls are just as varied, with the Book of Gates and the Book of Caverns in the corridors and the Book of the Earth in the burial chamber. And it has a human layer: hundreds of ancient graffiti, many of them Greek, left by Greco-Roman visitors who thought this was the tomb of Memnon. Very few modern visitors read far enough to notice.

Is Nefertari's tomb open? (QV66)

No, according to the latest reports. The Tomb of Nefertari in the neighbouring Valley of the Queens is reported closed since March 2024, with no reopening date, and we found no official notice either way. Some older pages still say it is open, so treat any page that promises a visit with caution. Its painted plaster is among the finest colour surviving from ancient Egypt, and it would be worth a place in your day if it reopens. Until then, plan without it; Seti I is the nearest thing to it in the Valley of the Kings.

How we fit them into a day

A west-bank day has one good shape, because the heat and the coaches decide most of it. This is how we would plan a morning with the extra tickets:

  1. 06:00: Valley of the Kings at opening. Buy your tickets at the Visitor Centre, because they are not sold past the tram, and carry a card, which is effectively required. Seti I first, Ramesses VI second, while the valley is still cool and quiet.
  2. 08:30: Tutankhamun, then the general ticket's tombs. KV62 is a short visit; the general ticket covers three more, chosen that morning for which are open and quiet.
  3. 10:00: out of the valley, into the shade. Deir el-Medina or the Temple of Hatshepsut while the light is still workable.
  4. 13:00: lunch and an afternoon reset before Karnak or Luxor Temple on the east bank after four.

Tombs close from time to time, so check the open list close to the day. None of these is a special-permit tomb. Permits are a different instrument for different doors: a permit and its cost are requested on booking and confirmed in writing before the balance is due, and if one is declined you hear from us and the journey is reshaped. The wider west bank, where to stay and how many days, is in the Luxor destination guide; how the seasons shape the choice is covered in when to go to Egypt.

FAQ

Which special tickets in the Valley of the Kings are worth paying extra for? Seti I (KV17), Ramesses V and VI (KV9) and, once, Tutankhamun (KV62): for the relief, the ceilings and the king himself. Confirm open status before you go, because tombs close for conservation.

Is Nefertari's tomb open? It is reported closed since March 2024, with no reopening date. It is in the Valley of the Queens, not the Valley of the Kings. Check the week you travel.

Is Seti I's tomb worth it? If relief carving or the New Kingdom is why you came, yes: KV17 is the longest tomb in the valley, decorated in painted raised relief. It is also the valley's most expensive ticket, so first-time visitors with a single day sometimes put the money elsewhere.

How much do the extra tickets cost? As reported in November 2026 for foreign adults: Seti I EGP 2,000, Tutankhamun EGP 700, and Ramesses V and VI EGP 220, each on top of the Valley of the Kings ticket (EGP 750). Egypt revises ticket prices without much notice, so check egymonuments.gov.eg before travelling.

Does the general Valley of the Kings ticket include these tombs? No. The general ticket covers three of the open royal tombs; Seti I, Tutankhamun, and Ramesses V and VI each need a separate ticket.

How long can you stay inside each tomb? We found no published limit for the Valley of the Kings tombs, though crowds and supervision shape how long you stay. Ask your Egyptologist on the day.

Are tomb closures something to worry about? No, but plan around them. Royal tombs close for conservation, sometimes for long periods, so the open list can change between your booking and your visit. Check current status the week before, and hold the day's plan loosely.

The takeaway

All three extra tickets earn their price for the right visitor, and none is worth a rushed visit. The difference between the general ticket and the special ones is not crowd-avoidance: it is the finest relief in the valley, a painted sky, and the one king who never left.
